advanced.e: The Governor's discretion is textually confined to specific situations (e.g., special responsibilities for certain States under Articles like 371 provisions) and to situations of constitutional necessity recognised by convention and case law (like appointing a CM in a hung Assembly), not a general or roving discretionary power.

advanced.q: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the historical evolution of the Governor's office from a check on state autonomy?
o: The Government of India Act, 1935 had no provision for a Governor and the office was created for the first time by the Constitution of 1950

The office of Governor existed under British colonial administration and the Government of India Act, 1935, and was retained (with modification, removing overriding colonial-era special powers) in the 1950 Constitution as a constitutional head of the State
The Governor's office was introduced only by the 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956
The office of Governor is unique to India with no precedent in the colonial period
advanced.e: The office of Governor existed under the Government of India Act, 1935, wielding wide special/discretionary powers under colonial rule; the Constitution of 1950 retained the office but recast the Governor primarily as a constitutional head acting on ministerial advice, though some Centre-linked and discretionary elements were retained.

advanced.q: Which of the following is the most accurate statement about judicial scrutiny of the Governor's satisfaction while reserving a Bill for the President's consideration under Article 201?
o: The Governor's satisfaction in reserving a Bill is wholly immune from any judicial examination in all circumstances without exception

Courts have generally shown deference in this area, though egregious constitutional violations or mala fide exercise could, in principle, attract limited scrutiny, similar to the broader jurisprudence on discretionary gubernatorial powers
The President cannot ever withhold assent once a Governor reserves a Bill under Article 201
Reservation of Bills under Article 201 is mandatory for every Bill passed by a State Legislature
advanced.e: While courts generally show considerable deference to the Governor's/President's satisfaction in reserving or assenting to Bills, the broader jurisprudential trend (as seen in cases like B.P. Singhal) suggests that gross mala fide or unconstitutional exercise of such discretionary powers is not entirely beyond limited judicial scrutiny.

advanced.q: Which of the following correctly identifies why the Governor's role is often termed a 'lynchpin' of Centre-State relations, based on the design of the Constitution?
o: Because the Governor is directly elected by the people of the State and represents state interests exclusively against the Centre

Because the Governor, appointed by and removable at the pleasure of the President, simultaneously functions as the constitutional head of the State bound generally by ministerial advice, creating a structural link between the Union and the State
Because the Governor has no functional connection to the Union government whatsoever
Because only the Governor can amend the Constitution under Article 368
advanced.e: The Governor's dual position — a Union appointee bound by the pleasure doctrine, yet simultaneously the constitutional/executive head of the State expected to act on ministerial advice — structurally embeds the office as a link (or 'lynchpin') between Centre and State governance.

advanced.q: Which of the following best describes the position on whether the Governor can act purely on personal discretion in appointing a Chief Minister when a single party has secured a clear absolute majority in the State Assembly elections?
o: The Governor retains full personal discretion and may appoint any person of choice as Chief Minister regardless of majority support

By settled convention, the Governor has no real discretion in such a scenario and must appoint the leader of the party with a clear majority as Chief Minister; discretion becomes relevant mainly in situations of a hung Assembly or post-election ambiguity
The Governor must always refer the matter to the President for a decision
The Governor must dissolve the Assembly and order fresh elections whenever a single party wins a majority
advanced.e: Where a party secures a clear absolute majority, constitutional convention leaves the Governor with little or no real discretion — the leader of that party must be invited to form the government; genuine discretionary dilemmas for the Governor typically arise only in a hung Assembly or where post-poll alliances create ambiguity about majority support.

advanced.q: Which of the following best explains the significance of the phrase 'Governor shall not be liable to any proceedings in any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office' under Article 361?
o: It confers absolute immunity on the Governor personally, in perpetuity, even after leaving office, for any private wrongdoing unrelated to official duties

It confers immunity for official acts performed in the exercise of the powers and duties of the office, distinguishing this from the separate protections regarding personal criminal/civil proceedings during the term of office
It means the Governor can never be criticised by the media or Parliament
It was struck down as unconstitutional in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
advanced.e: Article 361 grants immunity to the Governor specifically for official acts done in exercise of the powers/duties of the office, which is conceptually distinct from (though related to) the separate clauses granting protection from personal criminal proceedings and requiring notice for civil proceedings during the term of office; it was not struck down in Rameshwar Prasad, which instead scrutinised the reasons behind an Assembly dissolution recommendation.
